title: Ant, Visa and Mastercard align on a Know-Your-Agent framework for autonomous commerce
subtitle: Three previously competing agent-identity protocols agree to interoperate as payment networks brace for AI agents projected to move $3–5 trillion in consumer commerce by 2030.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Ant International, Mastercard and Visa announced on September 10 a joint Know-Your-Agent (KYA) interoperability framework — a shared identity and accountability layer that lets an AI agent acting on a shopper's behalf be recognized across all three payment ecosystems without re-registering with each one. The framework rests on the three companies' previously separate agent protocols — Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol (TAP), Mastercard's Verifiable Intent, and Ant's Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP) — and defines a common set of verification signals, credentialing requirements, and revocation semantics that each network agrees to honor while keeping its own risk-decisioning stack intact.

The mechanism matters more than the branding. An AI shopping agent that clears KYA presents a cryptographically verifiable identity, an issuing operator, and a mandate scope; a merchant or acquirer can then run its own risk checks against those attestations rather than re-onboarding the agent from scratch. That collapses the current pattern — where an agent authorized for Visa is treated as untrusted the moment it hits a Mastercard rail — into a single agent-onboarding step. The three networks framed the design around a projection that autonomous agents will orchestrate US$3–5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030, a scale at which per-network agent registration is not operationally viable.

This is the payments industry converging on a pattern the AI industry has been circling for a year. Anthropic's Claude Commerce Agents (September 3), OpenAI's dsewiki incident (September 6), and the CISA/NSA/FBI advisory on distillation (September 10) all point at the same underlying problem: an agent's authority to act needs to be verifiable, revocable, and legible to systems it did not sign up with. KYA is the first cross-network commitment in that direction from institutions that clear real money — and it applies to any agent, from a Claude tool call to a Gemini shopping flow to a bespoke enterprise bot, so long as the operator can produce the attestations.

Takeaway for learners: agent authorization is going to be a career for the next five years, and the vocabulary is worth learning now. KYA reuses concepts from KYC (know-your-customer) but the trust unit is a running agent instance, not a person. If you are building anything that lets a model spend money, book travel, or act on user accounts, read Visa TAP, Mastercard Verifiable Intent, and Ant AMP side by side and ask which pieces the KYA framework standardizes — that comparison is the shape of the emerging job.
